# MORE ABOUT PAROTITIS

Suppurative Parotitis. Acute bacterial parotitis affects primarily elderly, malnourished, dehydrated or post-operative patients. Symptoms include fever, toxicity, and tender swelling along the mandible with purulent drainage from the parotid duct. Suppurative parotitis is usually unilateral whereas viral parotitis is usually bilateral. Pain is intense and aggressive, analgesic therapy is required. Progression of infection may lead to massive swelling of the neck, respiratory obstruction, septicemia and osteomyelitis of adjacent facial bones. Empiric antibiotics are required for coverage of Staphylococcus aureus if bacterial, and surgical drainage is usually necessary.

Chronic Parotitis. Parotitis is recurrent with intermittent acute exacerbations.

Chronic, low-grade bacterial infection results in functional destruction of the salivary gland. It may be confused with Sjogren's syndrome, a noninfectious illness. Therapy includes systemic antibiotics. Parotidectomy may eventually be required for patients with long-standing infection.

Viral Parotitis. Mumps parotitis is characterized by the rapid, painful swelling of one or both parotid glands within 2 to 3 weeks after exposure to the mumps virus. Mumps usually involves both parotid glands whereas bacterial parotitis is unilateral. Other viral causes of parotitis include influenza and enteroviruses.

Mumps parotitis usually resolves spontaneously in 5 to 10 days. Provide symptomatic relief of pain and fever and maintain hydration to prevent secondary bacterial infection.
